content: A single visit is sufficient to perform an Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) test, although patients may need to return for a second visit to receive the results. In contrast, skin testing using the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) or TB Skin Test (TBST) is less expensive and can be conducted in field settings. However, it requires a cold chain for storage, two healthcare visits, and trained personnel skilled in intradermal injection, as well as reading and interpreting the results. One practical advantage of IGRAs over TST is that they are not affected by the booster response, which can necessitate a two-step testing process when TST reactivity diminishes over time since the initial infection. In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) expanded its list of recommended IGRAs to include Beijing Wantai’s TB-IGRA and QIAGEN’s QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus. The 2022 WHO recommendations reviewed three specific TBST products: Cy-Tb (Serum Institute of India, India), Diaskintest® (Generium, Russian Federation), and C-TST (formerly known as the ESAT6-CFP10 test, Anhui Zhifei Longcom, China). Users of these tests may need to provide appropriate guidance and explain the differences between TST and TBST. Like TST, TBST requires a cold chain, skilled staff for administration and interpretation, and multi-use vials for efficient operational planning and batching. Procurement and stock management, including global market availability, should also be considered, as TBSTs are relatively new in vivo tests and may require regulatory approval from national or other relevant authorities. It is important to note that TST, TBST, and IGRA are not validated for confirming active tuberculosis (TB) disease and should not be used for diagnosing TB or evaluating adults for TB disease. Preventive treatment for TB infection caused by drug-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains can be broadly categorized into two types: monotherapy with isoniazid for at least six months (IPT) and regimens containing a rifamycin (rifampicin or rifapentine). While IPT has been the most widely used form of TB preventive treatment (TPT), shorter rifamycin-based regimens offer clear advantages and are increasingly preferred. For multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), a different approach is required, primarily involving levofloxacin. Recommendations for these treatment options and their specific conditions are discussed in detail. The following TPT regimens are recommended regardless of HIV status: six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. These recommendations are strongly supported by moderate-to-high certainty evidence. Alternative TPT regimens include a one-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin. These alternatives are conditionally recommended based on low-to-moderate certainty evidence. Shorter regimens containing rifamycins, such as three months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP) or three months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin (3HR), are strongly recommended as alternatives to six months of daily isoniazid monotherapy (6H). Evidence from systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) supports the efficacy and safety of these shorter regimens. For example, 3HP has been shown to have similar effectiveness to isoniazid monotherapy, with higher treatment completion rates and a favorable safety profile. Additionally, 3HR has demonstrated comparable efficacy and safety to six months of isoniazid in both adults and children. The one-month daily rifapentine plus isoniazid regimen (1HP) has also been evaluated in a randomized, open-label, phase 3 non-inferiority trial. This regimen was found to be non-inferior to nine months of isoniazid monotherapy (9H) in people with HIV aged 13 years or older. However, due to limited data, 1HP is currently recommended only for individuals aged 13 years or older. Self-administered TPT regimens are feasible and preferred by many patients, as demonstrated by recent studies comparing self-administered and directly observed treatment for 3HP. Direct observation requirements may pose barriers to implementation, and individuals receiving TPT should be supported with advice on treatment adherence and management of adverse events. Drug-drug interactions are an important consideration when prescribing rifamycin-containing regimens, as these drugs can induce cytochrome P-450 enzymes, potentially interfering with the metabolism of other medications, including antiretroviral therapy (ART). For example, rifampicin and rifapentine can reduce the concentrations of boosted protease inhibitors and nevirapine, making co-administration inadvisable. However, 3HP has been shown to be safe and effective when co-administered with efavirenz-based ART regimens without dose adjustment. When rifampicin is used with dolutegravir, the dolutegravir dose must be increased to 50 mg twice daily. Pregnancy presents unique considerations for TPT. While rifampicin is generally considered safe during pregnancy, there is limited data on the pharmacokinetics and safety of rifapentine in pregnant women. As a result, 3HP and 1HP are not recommended during pregnancy until more information becomes available. Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) can be used during pregnancy, but baseline liver function testing is strongly encouraged, and routine vitamin B6 supplementation should be considered to prevent peripheral neuropathy. For individuals exposed to MDR/RR-TB, six months of daily levofloxacin is strongly recommended as TPT. This recommendation is based on moderate-certainty evidence from RCTs and systematic reviews. The use of levofloxacin for TPT aims to reduce the risk of secondary MDR/RR-TB cases, which are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality. In summary, the WHO guidelines provide a range of TPT options tailored to different populations and settings. Shorter rifamycin-containing regimens are increasingly preferred due to their higher completion rates and comparable efficacy to longer isoniazid monotherapy.
